messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T19

## Claude Opus 5.5


# T19 — Microgravity bulk-solids handling and comminution: TRL assessment

## Scope and assumptions

The two requirement statements describe the same mass balance with different scope.

- **GPT's version:** 2–8 kt/yr concentrate plus 13–47 kt/yr tailings, i.e. 15–55 kt/yr total.
- **Claude's version:** the same 15–55 kt/yr feed, plus crushing and milling to sub-mm and a ≥5-yr wear life.

I rate the union of both statements. The sub-functions are:

1. Metering and feeding without gravity.
2. Enclosed conveying and transfer.
3. Buffering and storage, including bridging and arching.
4. Charging and discharging of process vessels.
5. Comminution to sub-mm.
6. Size classification.
7. Tailings compaction and containment.
8. Upset recovery from jams, plugs and wall build-up.
9. Wear over 5 years.

**Derived rate**

- 15–55 kt/yr equals 1.7–6.3 t/h if run continuously.
- At an assumed 70% plant availability, design rate is roughly **2.4–9 t/h**.
- Excavation is batchy (robot duty cycle 9–25%), so buffering is required, not optional.

**Containment implication of D-03**

- The interim escape ceiling is ≤1 t/yr per site.
- Against 13–47 kt/yr of tailings, that is an escape fraction of about 2×10⁻⁵ to 8×10⁻⁵.
- That means roughly **99.998% retention summed over every transfer point**, before considering excavation ejecta.
- This makes enclosed handling the main debris control, not just a process convenience.

**Environment**

- Vacuum, at or near microgravity (10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ m/s² at the NEA), or 0.05–0.15 g inside a rotating module (Gemini route).
- Abrasive, tribo- and photo-charged regolith: fines from friable C-type material, metal-bearing clasts from S/M-type material.
- 0.9–1.3 AU thermal cycling.
- 5-yr life.

**Routes**

The metallurgy route changes the handling problem, so I rate it per route (below). One point applies to all routes: excavation and transfer to the plant are microgravity handling in every case, even if processing is spun.

**On the supplied literature reviews**

- The rq-0-6 and rq-0-9 reviews contain arXiv-ID citations and quantitative claims I cannot verify, for example "10s of W per kg/h" for bucket wheels.
- I do not use them as evidence. Where I cite a paper below, it is one I am reasonably confident exists.
- The rq-0-6 background figures (20 robots, 1,000+ t/robot/yr) are superseded by the revised architecture.

---

## 1. Evidence

### In-space and reduced-gravity heritage, all far below required scale

| # | Claim | Source | Demonstrated | Ratio to required | Confident |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | Gas-fluidised capture of loose regolith into a collector in microgravity. Upset observed: the collector's mylar flap was wedged open by particles and material leaked. | OSIRIS-REx TAGSAM, Bennu, Oct 2020. 121.6 g returned 2023. | Hundreds of grams in a ~6 s contact, once. Momentary rate ≈0.1–0.2 t/h. | Annual mass ~10¹¹. Rate ~15–90×. Duration ~3×10⁷× (6 s vs 5 yr). | Yes (mass and flap event). No (exact collected mass and rate). |
| E2 | Projectile-impact sampling into a horn and catcher in microgravity. | Hayabusa2, Ryugu, 2019. ~5.4 g returned 2020. | Grams, two events. | ~10¹³ | Yes |
| E3 | Granular convection and shear behaviour in reduced gravity measured in a Couette-type shear cell. | Murdoch et al. 2013, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* "Granular convection in microgravity". Parabolic flight. | Lab cell, ~20 s parabolas. | n/a. Physics data, not a handling device. | Yes |
| E4 | Triaxial compression of sand at very low confinement in orbit. | Mechanics of Granular Materials (MGM), Space Shuttle, STS-79 (1996) and STS-89 (1998). | Small specimens. | n/a. Constitutive data only. | Mostly. Flight list not verified. |
| E5 | Long-duration passive regolith-simulant segregation and behaviour on ISS. | Strata-1 (NASA JSC; Fries et al.). | Small sealed tubes, months, no active handling. | n/a | Existence yes. Dates and results summary no. |
| E6 | Low-velocity collisions of particles and aggregates in microgravity. | NanoRocks on ISS (Brisset, Colwell et al., mid-2010s). | mm–cm particles in small cells. | n/a | Partly |
| E7 | Pneumatic regolith sampling on the lunar surface (1/6 g, vacuum). | Honeybee Robotics Lunar PlanetVac, Firefly Blue Ghost M1 (2025). MMX P-Sampler for Phobos not yet flown. | Grams–tens of grams, minutes, partial gravity. | ~10¹¹. Wrong gravity regime. | Payload manifest yes. Operational results no. |
| E8 | Abrasive regolith degrades seals, mechanisms and fabrics within days of exposure. | Gaier 2005, NASA/TM-2005-213610, "The Effects of Lunar Dust on EVA Systems During the Apollo Missions". | Hours to days, 1/6 g, crewed. | Duration ~10³× | Yes |
| E9 | Metal-on-metal adhesion and cold welding under vacuum fretting and impact. | ESA cold-welding assessment, Merstallinger et al. (~2009, ESA STM series). | Coupon tests. | n/a. Wear-mechanism data. | Existence yes. Number and date no. |

### Terrestrial heritage at TRL 9, mostly gravity-reliant

- **Jenike-method hopper and flow design** (Jenike 1964, Utah Eng. Exp. Station Bulletin 123). Confident.
  - Critical outlet dimension for cohesive arching scales roughly as σ_c/(ρg).
  - This is directly relevant to the rotating route: at 0.1 g, cohesive-arch outlets are ~10× larger than at 1 g.
  - In true microgravity the method gives no answer.
- **Force-driven, nominally orientation-independent equipment** exists at t/h scale and above:
  - screw and auger feeders, rotary-valve and piston metering;
  - dense-phase pneumatic conveying (needs a carrier gas, so a closed gas loop in vacuum);
  - high-pressure grinding rolls;
  - stirred-media and vibratory mills.
  - None has been qualified for operation without gravity-assisted feed or discharge. Industrial mills feed and discharge by gravity.
- **Ball, rod, AG and SAG mills** depend on gravity cascading. They are not transferable to microgravity. They are partly transferable to a 0.1 g centrifuge with large redesign.

### What does not exist

I am aware of none of the following:

- an in-space demonstration of continuous bulk-solids transfer above the gram–kilogram scale;
- any in-space comminution;
- any in-space size classification;
- vacuum-plus-microgravity wear data for handling equipment.

I am not certain no small ISS powder-handling experiment exists. I know of none relevant to abrasive regolith at process scale.

---

## 2. Current TRL: **2–3**

Ratings by sub-function in microgravity, which is the no-melt and native-metal path:

| Sub-function | TRL | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Positive-displacement metering and conveying (screw, piston) | 3 | Mechanism is force-driven. Analysis is credible, and E3/E4 give constitutive inputs. No validated prediction exists for cohesive, charged fines without body force. |
| Closed-loop pneumatic transfer | 2–3 | E1 and E7 show gas mobilisation at grams. No loop-closure or gas-recovery data in vacuum. |
| Buffering, bridging, charging and discharge of vessels | 2 | No validated flow theory for zero-body-force storage. Bennu-like fines with high cohesion to weight are worst-case. |
| Comminution to sub-mm | 2 | Concept formulated (HPGR or stirred mill, force-fed and force-discharged). No proof-of-concept of feed and discharge without gravity. |
| Size classification | 2 | Screens rely on gravity or vibration. Alternatives proposed (centrifugal classification, gas classification) are unvalidated for this feed. |
| Tailings compaction and containment at 99.998% | 2 | Concept only. E1 is a direct counter-example: a single particle wedge defeated a seal. |
| Upset recovery | 2 | No data. |
| 5-yr wear | 2–3 | Terrestrial abrasion indices and E8/E9 bound the mechanisms. No relevant-environment life data. |

Rotating route (0.05–0.15 g):

- **2–3** for in-module handling. Jenike-type design applies in principle, but cohesive arching worsens by ~1/g, Coriolis effects distort chute and hopper flow, and no partial-g handling data exist below lunar g.
- **2** for transferring solids from a non-rotating to a rotating frame across a sealed interface in vacuum. This interface is not needed by the other routes and has no heritage I know of.

**Overall rating**

- **Lower bound, TRL 2 met.** Documented application concepts exist: the round-2 mass balances and the industrial equipment classes listed above.
- **Upper bound, TRL 3 partly met.** Only for force-driven conveying, supported by analysis plus E3/E4 constitutive data.
- **Unmet for TRL 3 overall.** There are no documented experimental results validating predictions of the key parameters for cohesive, charged, abrasive regolith with no or low body force:
  - feeder mass-flow versus speed;
  - plug and bridge onset;
  - wall build-up rate;
  - mill throughput and product size with forced discharge.
- **Also unmet for TRL 4.** There is no documented definition of the relevant environment for the handling train, specifically:
  - Bond-number range;
  - charge state;
  - particle size distribution and clast fraction by target type.

---

## 3. Target and difficulty

### Is it project-ending for 0B?

Yes. Co-located processing that ships product rather than ore needs every sub-function except possibly comminution. Tailings containment is also tied to the D-02 licence gate through D-03.

### Targets under D-02

- **0A mid-term review:** TRL 4, as an internal 0A milestone.
  - Ground breadboards of each sub-function, run orientation-independent in vacuum with flow-characterised simulants.
- **KDP-0B:** TRL 6 in a relevant environment, no waivers.
  - The KDP-0B date is not given in the material supplied. I state it as a milestone, not a year.
  - TRL 6 cannot be earned on the ground. Sustained microgravity is the defining condition, and parabolic flight (~20 s) or suborbital flight (~3 min) cannot show steady-state flow, wall build-up or upset recovery.
  - It therefore needs a flight subsystem prototype (free-flyer, or a 0A pathfinder payload) running for months.
  - It also needs a documented scaling argument from that subscale up to 2.4–9 t/h.

### AD² = 6

"Several competing approaches; the path is not clear."

- Metering and conveying alone would be **AD² 5**: the path is clear, the steps are new development.
- Bridging-free buffering, forced-discharge comminution, 99.998% containment and autonomous upset recovery have competing approaches with no basis to choose yet:
  - screw versus closed-loop pneumatic versus spin-assisted versus vibratory or electrostatic transport;
  - HPGR versus stirred mill versus none.
- The flight-test step itself is new.
- I would move to **AD² 7** if ground breadboards show that cohesive Bennu-like fines wall-plate continuously in vacuum regardless of transport method.

### Years to target

**6–12 years** from programme start:

- 2–3 years to TRL 4;
- 2–3 years more to TRL 5;
- 3–6 years for a flight prototype, including build, launch and months of operation.

---

## 4. Path

Costs are my order-of-magnitude estimates, not quotes.

Couplings:

- P2/P3 should share hardware and simulant with rq-0-51 (separator yield) and rq-0-6 (excavation).
- Containment data feed rq-0-41 and D-03.

---

## 5. Risk and fallback

### Risk class: project-ending for 0B

There are graded partial outcomes short of full failure:

- **Comminution fails, transfer works.** Architecture change: restrict to targets and products that need only coarse liberation, such as native Fe-Ni clasts or coarse metal from S/M-type material, and accept a lower concentration ratio. This risks the 3:1 falsifier in rq-0-51.
- **Microgravity handling fails, spun handling works.** Architecture change to Gemini's rotating module, which adds the rotating-interface risk.
- **Containment cannot be shown at ≤1 t/yr.** This is a licence-gate failure, which D-02 treats as project-ending for 0B.
- **All fail.** Pre-committed D-02 fallback: 0A only, with Earth supply.

Reopening ore shipping would reverse the co-location decision. It would be an architecture change requiring panel reconciliation, not a fallback.

---

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Whether the upper bound is TRL 3.** Someone could credit TRL 3 to the force-driven sub-functions on the strength of terrestrial physics plus E3/E4. I do not credit it for the system, because the hard functions (bridging, wall plating, forced mill discharge) lack any validated prediction. Equally, someone could argue TRL 1–2 for comminution, since there is no peer-reviewed work specific to microgravity milling that I can cite.
2. **Whether a 10–100 kg/h flight loop can earn TRL 6 for a 2.4–9 t/h plant.** That is a 25–900× scale-up. I accept it only with a DEM scaling law validated across P2–P3. A strict reading of "no waivers" might demand a larger flight article, which would push past the 0A budget.
3. **Whether ground testing can substitute for microgravity.** Advocates of orientation-independent equipment may argue that inverted 1 g tests plus cohesive simulants suffice for TRL 5–6. I disagree for steady-state storage and wall build-up. Cohesion-to-weight can be raised on the ground, but the absence of any preferred body-force direction cannot be reproduced.
4. **Gemini's rotating route.** The likely counter-argument is that 0.1 g makes conventional chutes and hoppers work. My objection is that cohesive arching and outlet sizing scale ~1/g, Coriolis effects distort flow, and the static-to-rotating solids interface is unprecedented. The route may still win, but it is not lower-risk on handling.
5. **Whether sub-mm comminution is required at all.** GPT's narrow native-metal scope may avoid it. Claude's no-melt carbonyl/H₂ route probably needs it. This is unresolved and depends on target sampling under the D-02 target gate.
6. **Wear.** I treat 5-yr wear as demonstrable only by accelerated ground test plus in-flight trend data. Others may say no pre-KDP-0B evidence can close it, and that it should be carried as a cost/schedule risk with replaceable liners rather than gating TRL.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


**1. Evidence**
Microgravity bulk-solids handling and comminution are notoriously difficult due to the dominance of cohesive (van der Waals) and electrostatic forces over gravity, leading to jamming, bridging, and persistent dust clouds. 
- **Granular behavior in microgravity:** Parabolic flight experiments (e.g., D'Angelo et al., 2022) and ISS experiments (e.g., Strata-1, 2016) have investigated granular compaction, force chains, and long-term settling of regolith simulants in microgravity. These operate at the scale of grams to a few kilograms.
- **Bulk conveying and comminution:** There is no physical demonstration of continuous enclosed transfer, metering, buffering, or crushing/milling of abrasive rock to sub-millimeter sizes in microgravity. Terrestrial systems rely heavily on gravity for material feed and clearing.
- **Scale ratio:** Required throughput is 15–55 kt/yr (roughly 1.7–6.3 t/h). Demonstrated microgravity handling is at the batch scale of <1 kg. The scale ratio is >10,000:1.

**2. Current TRL**
Current TRL is **2–3**. The physics of granular materials in microgravity are being actively researched (TRL 3 for basic behavior), but the specific application of continuous bulk conveying, metering, and comminution at scale lacks experimental proof-of-concept for key characteristics (TRL 2). The unmet exit criterion for TRL 3 is documented analytical or experimental results validating predictions of key parameters for continuous flow and crushing in microgravity.

**3. Target and difficulty**
Target TRL for KDP-0B is **6**, as failure to handle and process bulk solids renders the entire in-space production architecture unviable (project-ending). The Advancement Degree of Difficulty (AD²) is **7** (Requires new approaches; fundamental engineering research). Terrestrial bulk handling relies on gravity; replacing it with pneumatic, mechanical, or centrifugal forcing while managing extreme wear and electrostatic charging over 5 years requires fundamental engineering research.

**4. Path**
- **Simulation:** High-fidelity DEM modeling of enclosed conveyors, metering valves, and crushers incorporating electrostatic and cohesive forces (TRL 3).
- **Experiment (Parabolic/Drop Tower):** Sub-scale (10–100 kg/h) breadboard testing of transfer and metering mechanisms in parabolic flights to validate DEM (TRL 4).
- **Experiment (LEO Free-flyer / Pathfinder):** Continuous operation of a scaled-down (0.1–1 t/h) handling and comminution loop in sustained microgravity to prove upset recovery, wear resistance, and dust containment (TRL 5–6).

**5. Risk and fallback**
Risk if fail: **project-ending**. Without the ability to reliably move, buffer, and crush regolith, co-located processing cannot occur.
Fallback: 0A only, Earth supply.

**6. Where others might disagree**
The AD² rating of 7 might be contested by those who believe pneumatic conveying or simple augers can be easily adapted to microgravity. However, the requirement to handle highly abrasive, irregularly sized, electrostatically charged clasts while performing comminution (which generates immense dust and requires high forces) introduces severe jamming and wear risks that have never been solved in space.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


# T19 — Microgravity bulk-solids handling and conditional comminution

**Current TRL: 2–3 for the architecture-required subsystem. Target: TRL 6 before KDP-0B. AD²: 6.**

Small-sample capture and manipulation in asteroid gravity are flight-demonstrated. That does **not** establish continuous enclosed feeding, metering, buffering, tailings transfer, autonomous blockage recovery, or five-year wear performance at industrial throughput. Gravity-independent sub-mm comminution is an additional, less-supported requirement—not something demonstrated by asteroid sample-return missions.

The revised architecture removes bulk ore shipment but **does not remove bulk handling at the asteroid**. Tailings remain the dominant solids stream.

## 1. Assessment boundary and required scale

I assess material handling from the enclosed excavation/processing handoff through feed preparation, beneficiation interfaces, concentrate storage and tailings placement. Excavation, separation performance and metallurgy need their own assessments; T19 must nevertheless demonstrate their material interfaces.

Assumptions:

- Gross feed is **15–55 kt/yr**, with approximately **2–8 kt/yr concentrate and 13–47 kt/yr tailings**. These are correlated balances, not independently selectable endpoints.
- Five years means **75–275 kt cumulative gross feed**, unless KDP-0B explicitly adopts replaceable wear cartridges or shorter-lived modules.
- Sub-mm preparation is mandatory for the Claude variant as stated. It is **not automatically imposed on the other routes** without liberation and feed-acceptance evidence.
- Site handling remains in asteroid gravity unless a rotating enclosure deliberately supplies acceleration. A rotating furnace does not supply gravity to upstream bins or external tailings transfers.

| Stream | Annual requirement | Calendar-average mass flow |
|---|---:|---:|
| Gross feed | 15–55 kt/yr | 0.48–1.74 kg/s |
| Concentrate | 2–8 kt/yr | 0.063–0.254 kg/s |
| Tailings | 13–47 kt/yr | 0.41–1.49 kg/s |

Operating flow is calendar-average flow divided by plant availability. **The robots’ 9–25% duty cycle is not necessarily the plant duty cycle.** If imposed on the plant, gross operating flow would span roughly **1.9–19 kg/s**.

The relevant environment includes vacuum, target asteroid gravity, representative abrasive and cohesive feed, triboelectric charging, credible external plasma/UV exposure at openings, thermal boundary conditions for 0.9–1.3 AU, and accumulated radiation effects on controls and materials. Enclosed material is not necessarily continuously UV-exposed.

## 2. Evidence supporting—and limiting—the rating

The following are physical heritage, not design-study endorsements.

| Programme/test/paper | Demonstrated scale and environment | Required ÷ demonstrated scale | What it establishes—and does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OSIRIS-REx TAGSAM**, Bennu sampling, **2020**; NASA final sample inventory, **2024** | One short gas-assisted collection event in asteroid gravity and vacuum; **121.6 g** returned | One year gross feed ÷ returned inventory: **1.2×10⁸–4.5×10⁸**. Throughput ratio: **not comparable** | Material can be captured in asteroid gravity. The collection-head flap was held open by particles and material escaped before stowage. This is relevant upset/containment evidence, not a continuous conveyor demonstration. |
| **Hayabusa2 sampler**, Ryugu sampling, **2019**; JAXA returned-sample inventory, **2020** | Two brief sampling events in asteroid gravity and vacuum; approximately **5.4 g** returned | One year gross feed ÷ returned inventory: **2.8×10⁹–1.0×10¹⁰**. Throughput ratio: **not comparable** | Projectile-assisted acquisition and sample retention worked. No sustained metering, buffering, milling or tailings handling was demonstrated. |
| **Curiosity CHIMRA**, Mars operations from **2012**; Anderson et al., *“Collecting Samples in Gale Crater, Mars; an Overview of the Mars Science Laboratory Sample Acquisition, Sample Processing and Handling System,”* **Space Science Reviews, 2012** | Small, intermittent scoop/drill-powder processing, sieving and delivery; nominal **150 µm** fine-sieve aperture; Mars gravity and atmosphere | Industrial mass-flow and lifetime ratios: **n/a** without a specific operational batch/mass record | Strong heritage for instrument-scale powder processing and portion delivery. Mars gravity is about **3.7×10⁵–3.7×10⁶** the supplied asteroid-gravity range. Sieving drill-generated powder is not gravity-independent bulk milling. |
| **Phoenix TEGA sample-delivery operations**, NASA/JPL mission reports, **2008** | Small scoop samples delivered through screens on Mars; cohesive sample-delivery difficulties and vibration-assisted attempts | **n/a**: no comparable continuous throughput demonstrated | Physical evidence that even sample-scale transfer can be limited by adhesion and delivery geometry. Not a microgravity qualification. |
| **Brisset et al., 2018, Astronomy & Astrophysics**, *“Regolith behavior under asteroid-level gravity conditions: low-velocity impact experiments”*; COLLIDE/PRIME experimental heritage | Laboratory reduced-gravity granular impact experiments, including short-duration microgravity conditions | **n/a**: impact response, not sustained processing throughput | Test data constrain granular response and can calibrate models. They do not validate a feeder, buffer or mill. |

**Ratio caution:** returned mass is a verified inventory, not the complete mass disturbed or temporarily collected. The ratios expose the scale gap; they are **not** a throughput scaling law.

Terrestrial screw conveyors, positive-displacement feeders and enclosed mills establish useful engineering principles. I have not identified a documented test combining the required asteroid environment, continuous industrial feed, recovery functions and endurance. Their terrestrial maturity cannot be transferred wholesale to T19.

### Treatment of the supplied literature review

I would not use its unverified arXiv identifiers or categorical conclusions as rating evidence without checking the original publications and test records. In particular:

- Ordinary “vacuum suction” cannot collect material from an ambient vacuum without an introduced gas flow and a pressure differential.
- Vacuum does not itself imply zero mechanical overburden.
- Bennu bulk density is not interchangeable with loose-feed bulk density or individual grain density.
- Cohesion, charge and excavation-power claims cannot be generalized from carbonaceous material to the native-metal target without measurements.

The confidently identified flight programmes above are sufficient to establish relevant physical phenomena—but not industrial subsystem maturity.

## 3. Current TRL, keeping the routes separate

| T19 implementation | Current TRL | AD² to TRL 6 | Assessment |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Claude: no-melt route, including gravity-independent sub-mm comminution** | **2–3** overall; **2** for the specified continuous comminution implementation | **6** | The application is formulated. Sample-handling heritage supports selected functions, but I have no qualifying demonstration of the stated zero-gravity milling/feed/wear chain. Reduction or carbonyl chemistry is outside this T19 rating. |
| **Gemini: handling interfaces to a rotating 0.05–0.15 g smelting furnace** | **2–3** | **6** | Artificial gravity offers a plausible engineering route, but material entry, exit, spin-up, despinning and tailings handling remain unvalidated as an integrated subsystem. Furnace/metallurgical maturity must be rated separately. |
| **GPT: narrow native-metal production, enclosed transfer and experimentally gated rotating modules** | **2–3** | **5–6** | Avoiding unnecessary milling could simplify development. The lower difficulty applies only if sampled feed demonstrates adequate liberation without sub-mm crushing and representative rotating transfer tests succeed. Otherwise use AD² 6. |

For rotating handling, relevance requires more than matching nominal acceleration: rotation rate, radius, acceleration gradient, Coriolis effects, particle residence time and interface geometry matter.

### Exit criteria

- **Lower bound, TRL 2:** met by documented concepts for active enclosed handling and the stated application.
- **Upper bound, TRL 3:** defensible for selected critical handling functions using physical sample-acquisition and granular-test evidence. It is **not yet demonstrated for all architecture-critical functions**, especially continuous comminution and autonomous upset recovery.
- **Next unmet exit, TRL 4:** documented performance of a representative integrated laboratory breadboard agreeing with predictions, with the relevant environment defined. Required functions include feed, metering, buffering, bridging detection and clearance, containment, and—where required—comminution.
- **TRL 5–6 remain unmet:** no documented relevant-environment validation with scaling requirements, followed by a representative subsystem demonstration.

Thus **2–3 is an evidence-boundary range**, not an average of model opinions. A conservative review board could reasonably assign **TRL 2** to the complete T19 chain.

## 4. Target, timing and advancement difficulty

- **0A internal milestone:** TRL **4–5**, reached through ground breadboards and relevant-environment component testing.
- **KDP-0B:** TRL **6**, without waiver, for the selected end-to-end solids route.
- **Needed by:** before committing to 0B production hardware. No calendar date for KDP-0B is supplied.
- **Planning duration:** approximately **6–10 years from funded start**, assuming overlapping development and a timely flight opportunity. This is a planning estimate, not demonstrated schedule performance.

**AD² 6** uses the project’s anchor: several competing approaches and no established path. The difficulty is engineering rather than uncertain basic physics: feed heterogeneity, cohesive fines, contact charging, rotating interfaces, bearing/seal protection and recoverable jams interact. Five-year cumulative wear is a major qualification burden.

## 5. Advancement path

Costs below are **rough-order-of-magnitude 2026 USD**, not supplier quotations. They cover T19-specific development; the flight line includes an allocated flight/platform provision, not the entire asteroid pathfinder mission. Work packages overlap, so durations should not be summed.

| Step | Method, scale and discriminating measurements | Cost | Duration | TRL reached |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Define feed and operating envelope** | Characterize candidate-target material and defensible analogues: particle-size distribution, metal liberation, cohesion, charge, hardness and abrasivity. Use kg-scale lots; define buffer capacity, plant availability and replaceability. | **$1–3M** | **0.5–1 yr** | **2**; definition alone does not raise hardware TRL |
| **Integrated laboratory breadboard** | Enclosed feeding–buffer–transfer–tailings chain; conditional crusher/mill. Approximately **0.01–0.1 kg/s**, tonnes cumulative. Inject oversize clasts, fines-rich feed, power loss and jams; compare measured performance with predictions. | **$3–10M** | **1–2 yr** | **4** |
| **Calibrated transport and wear models** | DEM and contact/charge models validated against tests; model rotating interfaces and scale-up. Measure liner, seal and bearing wear rather than relying on generic terrestrial factors. | **$1–4M** | **1–2 yr** | Supports **4–5**; no independent promotion from simulation alone |
| **Relevant-environment component campaign** | Vacuum/thermal/charging tests combined with reduced-gravity trials where necessary; approximately **0.01–0.3 kg/s**. Test sustained imposed partial gravity for rotating variants. Document similarity limits and scaling requirements. | **$5–15M** | **1.5–3 yr** | **5**, only if the relevant-environment case is demonstrated |
| **Long-duration microgravity pilot** | Hosted or free-flying prototype, or 0A asteroid pathfinder: roughly **0.01–0.1 kg/s**, hundreds of kg to several tonnes cumulative, months of repeated operations. Demonstrate closed-loop metering, buffer drawdown, restart, containment and autonomous jam clearance. | **$30–100M** | **3–5 yr**, including development | **5**, potentially **6 for a smaller pilot**; not automatically TRL 6 at production scale |
| **Production-representative qualification** | Selected module at its actual operating flow. For continuous operation, aggregate capacity **0.5–2 kg/s** covers the stated balance; intermittent operation needs more. Demonstrate integrated relevant-environment behaviour and validated scaling from the flight pilot; endurance campaign represents **75–275 kt** lifetime exposure or an explicitly accepted replaceable-module plan. | **$15–50M** | **3–5 yr**, overlapping pilot | **6**, conditional on accepted environment, scale and life evidence |

### Non-negotiable acceptance measurements

1. **Mass balance:** captured input, concentrate, tailings, retained inventory and escaped material—not merely nominal conveyor capacity.
2. **Containment:** allocating the entire interim **1 t/yr** site ceiling to gross-feed handling would permit only about **18–67 ppm escape by mass**. T19 receives only part of that budget. The **10 kg/yr aspiration** corresponds to approximately **0.18–0.67 ppm**.
3. **Recovery:** deliberate bridging, packing, stall, oversize and power-interruption tests, including recovery without ground intervention.
4. **Comminution where required:** product-size distribution, liberation, energy consumption, fines generation and throughput. A sieve aperture alone is insufficient.
5. **Lifetime:** measured wear laws, bounded extrapolation and demonstrated replacement/redundancy arrangements. Accelerated tests must preserve wear mechanisms; higher speed or harsher abrasive feed is not automatically valid acceleration.

An orbital pilot is valuable, but ISS plasma, thermal conditions and residual acceleration do not exactly reproduce an NEA site. Those differences require explicit justification.

## 6. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: project-ending for 0B if no solids-handling route reaches TRL 6.** This means ending the in-space production option, not ending 0A or Project Dyson.

Failure of **one implementation** can instead be an **architecture-change**:

- Replace zero-gravity transfer sections with enclosed rotating drums or cartridges.
- Reduce throughput or add parallel modules, subject to demand and economics gates.
- Select a target with adequately liberated native metal and avoid unnecessary comminution.
- Use replaceable wear components—but validate robotic replacement and revise logistics.

These are fallback concepts, **not mature substitutes**. If none passes the gate, invoke **“0A only, Earth supply.”**

## 7. Where others might disagree

- **TRL 2 versus 3:** the strongest disagreement is whether sample capture and granular tests validate enough of the production chain’s critical functions to satisfy TRL 3. They support selected functions, not the whole chain.
- **Credit for rotating hardware:** some assessors may give terrestrial enclosed feeders and mills substantial credit once artificial gravity is introduced. That is reasonable only for hardware whose force field and interfaces are genuinely reproduced.
- **Whether sub-mm milling is required:** liberation testing could remove it from the native-metal route. That lowers scope and difficulty; it does not retroactively mature the specified Claude implementation.
- **Lifetime interpretation:** five-year plant service with qualified replacement modules is different from five-year life of every wear surface. KDP-0B must specify which requirement applies.

# T19 Consolidated Rating: Microgravity Bulk-Solids Handling and Comminution

**Rapporteur's note.** This record attributes every position to the model that holds it. Where models diverge, the record does not rule; it names the test or source that would settle the point. The few rapporteur checks are limited to re-running arithmetic from figures the models themselves stated.

---

## 1. Summary table

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current TRL** | 2–3. Sub-functions mostly 2; force-driven conveying up to 3. Static-to-rotating interface 2. | 2–3. Basic behaviour 3; application 2. | 2–3. Comminution 2. Says a conservative board "could reasonably assign TRL 2" to the full chain. |
| **AD²** | 6. Would be 5 for metering and conveying alone; moves to 7 if breadboards show continuous wall-plating. | **7** ("fundamental engineering research"). | 6. Gives 5–6 for the narrow native-metal route if liberation evidence removes milling. |
| **Target** | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waivers. TRL 4 at 0A mid-term. | TRL 6 at KDP-0B. No 0A milestone given. | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waiver. TRL 4–5 as 0A internal target. |
| **Risk class** | Project-ending for 0B, with graded architecture-change outcomes. | Project-ending. | Project-ending for the in-space production option (not for 0A); single-route failure is an architecture change. |
| **Years to target** | **6–12** | **4–7** | **6–10** |
| **Self-stated confidence** | Low | **High** | Medium |
| **Fallback** | 0A only, Earth supply. Interim options: spun handling or coarse-liberation scope. | 0A only, Earth supply. | 0A only, Earth supply. Interim options: rotating drums or cartridges, parallel modules, liberated native-metal target, replaceable wear parts. |

---

## 2. Where the models agree

- **Current TRL band.** All three rate the full chain 2–3, and none claims TRL 3 is met for the complete chain.
  - Claude and Gemini name TRL 3 as the unmet exit criterion.
  - GPT names TRL 4 as the next unmet criterion but states that "complete-chain TRL 3 evidence also remains incomplete."
- **Comminution maturity.** Where comminution is in scope, all three rate it at or near TRL 2. None knows of any in-space comminution or continuous bulk transfer above the gram–kilogram scale.
- **Target and gating.** All three set TRL 6 by KDP-0B and treat failure as project-ending for 0B. All three name "0A only, Earth supply" as the terminal fallback.
- **Calendar-average throughput.** All three use 15–55 kt/yr, equal to 1.7–6.3 t/h. GPT's 0.48–1.74 kg/s is the same range.
- **Terrestrial heritage does not transfer.** All three say terrestrial bulk-handling heritage is gravity-reliant and cannot be carried over wholesale.
- **Tailings drive the problem.** Claude and GPT state that the revised architecture removes ore shipment but not bulk handling at the asteroid. Tailings are the dominant stream, and site handling stays in asteroid gravity even if processing is spun.
- **Containment budget.** Claude and GPT both derive a retention requirement of order 10⁻⁵ escape fraction from the ≤1 t/yr ceiling. The figures agree once their denominators are aligned:
  - Claude: 2–8×10⁻⁵ against tailings.
  - GPT: 18–67 ppm against gross feed. GPT adds that T19 receives only part of that budget, and that the 10 kg/yr aspiration implies 0.18–0.67 ppm.
- **TAGSAM as upset evidence.** Claude and GPT both cite the TAGSAM flap being wedged open by particles as direct evidence of containment upset.
- **Supplied literature reviews.** Claude and GPT both decline to use the unverified arXiv IDs and quantitative claims in the supplied reviews.
- **Path shape.** All three paths run from characterisation and modelling, through subscale testing, to a long-duration microgravity flight pilot.

---

## 3. Where the models diverge, and why

### D1. AD² is 6 (Claude, GPT) or 7 (Gemini)

- **Gemini** holds that replacing gravity with pneumatic, mechanical or centrifugal forcing, while managing wear and charging over 5 years, "requires fundamental engineering research." It cites the jamming and dust problems of comminuting charged, abrasive clasts.
- **GPT** states the difficulty is "engineering rather than uncertain basic physics."
- **Claude** sits between the two. It gives 6 because competing approaches exist with no basis yet to choose, and it names its own trigger for moving to 7.
- **What would settle it:** Claude's stated trigger. Orientation-independent vacuum breadboards with cohesive, Bennu-like fines (Claude P2; GPT's integrated breadboard) would show whether wall-plating occurs continuously regardless of transport method.

### D2. Years to target: 4–7 (Gemini) against 6–12 and 6–10 (Claude, GPT)

The gap follows from path structure rather than evidence.

- **Gemini** reaches TRL 4 through parabolic-flight breadboards and TRL 6 through a single free-flyer at 0.5 t/h.
- **Claude and GPT** insert ground vacuum breadboards, a separate relevant-environment campaign and wear testing.
  - Claude adds a separate rotating-route flight.
  - GPT adds a production-representative qualification step after the pilot.
- **Claude** argues that parabolic (~20 s) and suborbital (~3 min) flights cannot show steady-state flow, wall build-up or upset recovery. This bears directly on Gemini's TRL 4 step. Gemini does not address the point.
- **Rapporteur arithmetic:** Gemini's own step durations sum to 4–8 years if run sequentially, against its stated 4–7.
- **What would settle it:**
  - A panel ruling on whether short-duration reduced-gravity tests can satisfy TRL 4 or 5 exit criteria for steady-state functions.
  - A programme schedule built against an actual flight manifest. GPT conditions its estimate on "a timely flight opportunity."

### D3. Whether sub-mm comminution is in scope

- **Claude** rates the union of all requirement statements, so sub-mm comminution is included. Claude flags this as unresolved in its own disagreement section, item 5.
- **Gemini** treats comminution as required without qualification.
- **GPT** treats it as conditional: mandatory for the Claude no-melt variant only, and possibly removable for the native-metal route by liberation testing. GPT notes that removing it "does not retroactively mature the specified Claude implementation."
- **What would settle it:** liberation and feed-acceptance tests on target-representative material (GPT's feed-definition step; Claude's P1), tied to target sampling under the D-02 target gate (Claude).

### D4. Scale and environment needed to earn TRL 6

| Model | Flight article that reaches TRL 6 | Ratio to required rate | Condition attached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude | 10–100 kg/h loop in microgravity for 3–12 months | ~25–900× below required rate | Only with a DEM scaling law validated across P2–P3. Claude notes a strict "no waivers" reading might demand a larger article. |
| GPT | Pilot at 0.01–0.1 kg/s (≈36–360 kg/h) reaches **TRL 5**, "potentially 6 for a smaller pilot" | — | TRL 6 requires a further production-representative qualification at actual module flow (aggregate 0.5–2 kg/s), covering 75–275 kt lifetime exposure or a qualified replacement plan. |
| Gemini | 0.5 t/h free-flyer | — | Treated as reaching TRL 6 directly. |

- **What would settle it:** a KDP-0B ruling on the minimum demonstrated-to-required scale ratio, and on whether a validated scaling model is acceptable under "no waivers." Claude (§6 item 2) and GPT (§7) both raise this as open.

### D5. Whether ground testing can substitute for microgravity

- **Claude** says inverted 1 g tests with high-cohesion simulants cannot reproduce the absence of a preferred body-force direction. In Claude's view they are not sufficient for steady-state storage and wall build-up. Claude anticipates others will disagree.
- **GPT** uses vacuum, thermal and charging ground tests "combined with reduced-gravity trials where necessary." GPT also cautions that ISS plasma, thermal conditions and residual acceleration differ from an NEA site.
- **Gemini** goes from parabolic flight directly to free-flyer.
- **What would settle it:** paired comparison of the same breadboard in inverted-1 g cohesive-simulant tests and in sustained microgravity (the flight pilot). This tests whether ground results predict flight behaviour.

### D6. Treatment of the rotating route

- **Claude** rates the rotating route separately:
  - in-module handling at 2–3, citing ~1/g arching, Coriolis effects and no data below lunar g;
  - the static-to-rotating solids interface at 2, citing no heritage.
  - Claude budgets a separate spun-module flight (P6R).
- **GPT** rates the rotating-furnace handling interfaces at 2–3, AD² 6. GPT says relevance requires matching rotation rate, radius, gradient, Coriolis, residence time and geometry, not just nominal acceleration.
- **Gemini** does not address the 0.05–0.15 g route in its assessment.
- **What would settle it:** a sustained spun-module test that includes the static-to-rotating interface (Claude P6R; GPT "representative rotating tests").

### D7. Interpretation of the duty cycle

- **Claude** applies 70% plant availability to get a design rate of 2.4–9 t/h. Claude treats the robots' 9–25% duty cycle as making buffering mandatory.
- **GPT** says the robot duty cycle "is not necessarily the plant duty cycle." If it were imposed on the plant, gross flow would be 1.9–19 kg/s.
- **What would settle it:** a defined plant availability and buffer-capacity specification. GPT's feed-definition step includes this.

### D8. Whether simulation can promote TRL

- **Gemini** gives DEM first, reaching TRL 3.
- **Claude** places DEM after tests and pairs it with P3 to reach TRL 5.
- **GPT** says there is "no independent promotion from simulation alone."
- **What would settle it:** a panel convention on whether model-only results count toward TRL exit criteria.

### D9. Lifetime definition

- **Claude** requires ≥5-year wear life, shown by accelerated vacuum wear testing plus in-flight trend data. Claude notes others may prefer to carry wear as cost/schedule risk with replaceable liners.
- **GPT** distinguishes five-year plant service with replaceable modules from five-year life of every wear surface. GPT warns that accelerated tests must preserve wear mechanisms.
- **Gemini** folds wear into the flight demonstration.
- **What would settle it:** a KDP-0B specification of which lifetime requirement applies. Claude (§6 item 6) and GPT (§7) both call for this.

### D10. Confidence

- Gemini states **high** confidence while citing one evidence entry, and that entry depends on an arXiv ID of the kind the other two declined to use.
- Claude states **low** and GPT **medium**, with 9 and 5 evidence items respectively.
- The record preserves this spread without adjustment.

---

## 4. Evidence register

### Cited by more than one model

| OSIRIS-REx TAGSAM, Bennu 2020; 121.6 g returned | Claude, GPT | Both confident on mass and flap event. Claude unsure of exact collected mass and rate. | **Strongest shared evidence.** Relevant both as microgravity capture and as a containment-upset counter-example. |
| Hayabusa2, Ryugu 2019; ~5.4 g returned | Claude, GPT | Both confident | Acquisition only. No sustained handling. |
| Strata-1, ISS | Claude, Gemini | **Claude: unsure** ("dates and results no", late 2010s). **Gemini: confident**, dated 2016. | Date and results unverified across models. Settle with the NASA JSC/Fries et al. publication record. |

### Cited by one model only (flagged)

|---|---|---|
| Murdoch et al. 2013, *PRL*, granular convection, parabolic flight | Claude | No |
| Mechanics of Granular Materials, STS-79/STS-89 | Claude | **Yes** (flight list unverified) |
| NanoRocks, ISS (Brisset, Colwell et al.) | Claude | **Partly** (not carried into YAML) |
| Lunar PlanetVac on Firefly Blue Ghost M1, 2025 | Claude | **Yes** (operational results unknown) |
| Gaier 2005, NASA/TM-2005-213610, Apollo dust | Claude | No |
| Merstallinger et al., ESA cold-welding assessment | Claude | **Yes** (report number and date unverified) |
| Jenike 1964, Utah Eng. Exp. Station Bulletin 123 | Claude | No |
| D'Angelo et al. 2022, arXiv:2202.10792 | **Gemini** | No, but flagged here. Claude and GPT both declined to rely on unverified arXiv IDs from the supplied reviews. Needs independent verification before use. |
| Curiosity CHIMRA; Anderson et al. 2012, *Space Science Reviews* | GPT | No |
| Phoenix TEGA sample delivery, 2008 | GPT | Not marked; table only, not in YAML |
| Brisset et al. 2018, *A&A*, low-velocity impact at asteroid-level gravity | GPT | No (shares an author group with Claude's NanoRocks entry but is a different item) |

### Scale-ratio inconsistency (rapporteur arithmetic from the models' stated inputs)

For annual gross feed divided by returned mass, Claude and GPT give different figures for the same missions.

| Mission | Claude's figure | GPT's figure | Rapporteur recomputation |

### Acceptance measurements

The following are common to Claude and GPT. Gemini names upset recovery, wear and containment in general terms.

- **Mass-balance closure:** input, concentrate, tailings, retained inventory and escaped mass.
- **Containment:** verification against the allocated share of the ≤1 t/yr budget.
- **Upset recovery:** deliberate bridging, plugging, stall, oversize and power-loss tests, with autonomous recovery.
- **Comminution, where required:** product PSD, liberation, energy, fines generation and throughput (GPT).
- **Wear:** measured wear laws with bounded extrapolation.
